title: File:Boracay Island.jpg
desc: While only 7km tall and at its bikini line 500m wide, tiny Boracay is the Philippines' top tourist draw, fuelled by explosive growth and a tsunami of hype. The beach path is typically awash with visitors, including large groups of package tourists. The ocean is full of romantic paraws (an outrigger sailboat) giving rides; colourful parasails fill the air. After perfect sunsets, live music breaks out, and fire dancers twirl their batons.

title: File:Sailing into The Sunset, Boracay, Philippines.jpg
desc:
Boracay is a small island in the Philippines located approximately 315 km (196 mi) south of Manila and 2 km off the northwest tip of Panay Island in the Western Visayas region of the Philippines. Boracay Island and its beaches have received awards from numerous travel publications and agencies.  The island is administered by the Philippine Tourism Authority and the provincial government of Aklan. Apart from its white sand beaches, Boracay is also famous for being one of the world's top destinations for relaxation. It is also emerging among the top destinations for tranquility and nightlife.
In 2012, Boracay was awarded as the best island in the world from the international travel magazine Travel + Leisure.

title: File:Sugarcane harvesting in Batad.jpg
desc:
Sugarcane harvesting in Batad[1], Iloilo, Philippines.
Sugarcane harvesting  in the Philippines is mostly done by hand, with workers cutting the cane stalks at the base and then loading them into trucks for delivery to a processing plant. To ensure high sugarcane quality, farmers commonly use insecticides, herbicides, and fertilizers to control pests and diseases, as well as to increase yields. Harvesting usually takes place during the dry season, and sugarcane is harvested at the optimal stage of maturity.

title: File:Banaue Rice Terraces of the Philippines.jpg
desc:
The Banaue Rice Terraces is one of the renowned National Cultural Treasures of the
Philippines, not only known locally but also internationally because of its breathtaking beauty.
The rice terraces had been in the mountainous regions of Ifugao and northern Luzon for over 2
centuries. It soars around 1500 meters above sea level and it takes effort to see its beauty
because it is located in one of the remote parts of the Philippines; main island of Luzon. The
people of the Terraces have sustained its beauty by farming the area the same way their
ancestors carried it out for over a hundred years ago. However, there are threats that the
Banaue Rice Terraces face. The destruction of the rice terraces because of the natural calamity
and the continuous migration of the farmers to the cities hoping for better opportunities to
feed their families. Let us help conserve the heritage of one of the 8th Natural wonders of the
world, to not only see the Banaue rice terraces from photographs and textbooks but rather let

us put effort into the conservation of this natural treasure for the next generation, by conserving cultural heritage and creating authentic tourist experiences.

title: File:Heirloom rice from the Cordillera.jpg
desc:
Heirloom rice are seeds passed from generation to generation. The indigenous communities in uplands were able to sustain their terraced wet-rice cultivation and were protected from Spanish interference.
Heirloom rice is harvested using traditional farming methods especially in remote communities of the Cordilleras. Since these varieties grow in rice terraces in high elevations, they can only be planted and harvested manually with little to no help from carabaos or machinery. Moreover, maintaining the stonewalled terraces in the rugged and steep mountainous landscape is also an arduous task.
The planting of these rice varieties is also an intricate affair. Aromatic native varieties tend to attract rats in the field. Because of this, all aromatic varieties must be planted with a synchronized method within the area.

The indigenous peoples of the Cordilleras are deeply connected to their agricultural heritage. The heirloom rice varieties are the heart and soul of the terraces and have been part of their cultural practices for hundreds of years. Several of the planting sites of native rice have even been recognized as World Heritage Sites by UNESCO.

title: File:Rice Harvest in Asipulo.jpg
desc: In Asipulo, rice is typically grown in terraced fields, which are an iconic feature of the region. These rice terraces, like the famous Banaue Rice Terraces, are a living testament to the ingenuity and hard work of the Ifugao people. The terraces, built into the mountainside, have been maintained for centuries, often using traditional techniques passed down through generations, preserving a historical continuity that is truly remarkable.

title: File:Coconut spathe of Malayan Yellow Dwarf variety (Cocos nucifera).jpg
desc: This hybrid coconut plant tree is known as "Malayan Yellow Dwarf" variety a scientific name (Cocos nucifera). Grateful after 3 years and 3 months of taking care with giving enough water, organic and inorganic fertilizer for this dwarf coconut tree that thrives in full sunlight, planted in the backyard at home now shown the first development of spathe in life cycle. The unopened young coconut spathe surrounds and encloses the spadix to protect the developing flowers inside. It is located at the crown of the palm tree emerging from between the leaf bases attached to the trunk. A color pale, yellowish growth of spathe is in the height of about 30 cm.long and width 4 cm. in just 2 weeks as estimated from growing stage. Looking forward for this coconut spathe in the next few months if fortunately bear more fruits which believe to be naturally sweet and juicy. The dwarf coconut tree is not only perfect for landscaping but also among to be called the "tree of life" as uses for food, shelter and other materials to provide what we want and need in time.

title: File:Traditional Filipino Weaving and Cultural Heritage.jpg
desc: The image presents a museum exhibit dedicated to traditional Filipino weaving materials and processes, highlighting the creativity and craftsmanship of Indigenous communities in the Philippines. The display contains various woven textiles, colorful garments, traditional accessories, head coverings, ornaments, and other handmade objects. These artifacts demonstrate how natural materials were transformed into useful and meaningful items through traditional weaving techniques. The exhibit also emphasizes the cultural importance of weaving as a form of identity, artistic expression, and heritage. By preserving and displaying these objects, the museum helps visitors understand the skills, traditions, and histories passed down through generations of Filipino communities.

desc:

title: File:Hablon in the Kabilin Center.jpg
desc:
Hablon, a traditional handwoven fabric, is featured in the Kabilin Center to showcase the beauty of local craftsmanship and the historical significance of textile weaving in Cebu and the Philippines. The word "hablon" comes from the Cebuano term "habol", which means "woven fabric."
Culture and Tradition of Hablon
Hablon weaving is an ancient art practiced by traditional weavers in communities across Cebu and other parts of the Philippines. The materials used are often natural fibers such as abaca, piña, and cotton. The weaving process is intricate, requiring time, skill, and patience to create the fabric's unique patterns and designs.
Hablon at the Kabilin Center
At the Kabilin Center, Hablon is displayed to honor the local weavers who preserve the art of handwoven textiles. Visitors can admire hablon pieces featuring intricate designs and vibrant colors, often representing traditional motifs and Cebuano history.
A Legacy for the Community
Hablon is more than just a product; it is a symbol of the economic and cultural identity of Cebu's communities. It reflects the artisans' dedication to their craft and their ability to create unique and beautiful products that represent Filipino heritage on a global scale.
The Kabilin Center plays a vital role in preserving and promoting hablon, helping visitors and future generations appreciate its importance to the culture and history of Cebu.
Nanay Naring is often recognized as one of the significant figures in preserving the art of Hablon weaving, and her work may be featured or acknowledged in the Kabilin Center. Her dedication to this craft showcases the skill and artistry of traditional weavers in Cebu, highlighting their vital role in keeping this cultural heritage alive.
Nanay Naring and Hablon
Nanay Naring, like many traditional artisans, is part of a lineage of weavers who have passed down the knowledge and techniques of hablon weaving through generations. Her work involves creating intricate patterns using natural fibers, blending tradition with creativity. Each piece she creates tells a story of Cebu’s rich history and its connection to traditional crafts.
Hablon in the Kabilin Center
If Nanay Naring's creations are featured at the Kabilin Center, it serves as a tribute to her contributions to Cebuano culture. The center may display her woven fabrics as a way of honoring her craftsmanship and sharing her legacy with visitors. Her hablon pieces likely exhibit the vibrant colors, traditional designs, and meticulous workmanship characteristic of Cebuano handwoven textiles.

Nanay Naring’s role in the Kabilin Center underscores the importance of recognizing local artisans as cultural heroes who preserve and sustain Filipino traditions.

title: File:Bacbac- Leathery look from abaca outer stem.jpg
desc:
The leathery texture and the natural shiny brown hue of the bacbac or palacpac of Bulusan results to an elegant finish to this wide-brimmed hat made by a local weaver. The same weave style can be seen also in buri and karagumoy hats. Palacpac or bacbac is the dried stem covering of the abaca trunk that is harvested  while these are still attached to the plant. If not harvested these dried outer covering will just wither and decay in the abaca plant body.
The major product of abaca crop is  Manila hemp (fiber from abaca plant). These bacbac are just by-products while the abaca plant is not yet harvestable for hemp production.

Bulusan, Sorsogon, Philippines

File:Weaving Techniques and Textile Traditions of Mindanao.jpg
desc: Tie-dyed cloths, also known as ikat or bébéd, among the indigenous non-Moros in Mindanao and in some parts of eastern Indonesia was referred to by Alfred Bühler, a Swiss ethnologist, as the "most archaic" form of ikat weaving in the world. This technique is still employed by the indigenous non-Moro groups, mainly on abaca cloth, using warp-ikat decorations of zoomorphic, anthropomorphic, and geometric designs. Although ikat is more prominent in central and eastern Mindanao, some Moro groups also practice the ikat tradition, known as balod (wave) among the Maranao and binaludan among the Maguindanao. Other Maranao textiles employing the ikat weaving technique are the malong a andon (tubular cloth made of silk) and the tubao (headcloth).

desc:
Rattan and Nito are both materials commonly used in traditional crafts and furniture-making in the Philippines, including in areas like Badian and other parts of Cebu.
Rattan: This is a type of climbing palm that is widely used in the Philippines for furniture and handicrafts. Rattan is known for its flexibility and strength, making it ideal for weaving and crafting furniture such as chairs, tables, and baskets. Rattan furniture is lightweight yet durable, which makes it a popular choice for both indoor and outdoor decor.
Nito: Nito is a vine-like plant found in the Philippines, commonly used in weaving. It is often used to make baskets, hats, mats, and other handmade items. Nito is prized for its dark, glossy appearance and is used to create intricate and detailed woven designs. It’s a sustainable material that has been part of Filipino culture for generations.

Both rattan and nito are used in the making of traditional Filipino products and are often crafted by local artisans, who weave them into beautiful, functional items that showcase Filipino craftsmanship and culture. These materials are sometimes combined with pandan leaves to create even more intricate products such as mats, bags, and furniture.

title: File:Tultul Asin.jpg
desc: Artisanal salt blocks of Hoskyn, Guimaras. This salt is treated as a viand by locals. These salt blocks are produced by Emma and Serafin Ganila, two of the few remaining tultul salt masters of Guimaras. It is made with ashes of assorted driftwood (dagsa) doused with seawater for several days. Ashes are collected and placed in a filter called kaing, this serves as a strainer for new seawater. Strained water are boiled in hurnohan. The salt-makers add coconut milk to the liquid for added savory flavor.

title: File:Asin Tibuok, an artisanal salt from Alburquerque, Bohol.jpg
desc:
Asin tibuok is a rare artisanal salt from Alburquerque, Bohol made from filtering seawater through ashes. It has a sharp, salty flavor with mild smoky undertones.
The making of asin tibuok is labor-intensive. First, the saltmakers or asinderos soak the coconut husks in pits that catch seawater during high tides for several months. The husks are then cut into small pieces and dried under the sun for a few days. During the drying process, the coconut husks are not allowed to be rained on, or else the asinderos have to start from scratch.  The dried husks are then burned and reduced to ashes called gasang. The asinderos collect the gasang and then put it in a funnel-shaped bamboo filtering device called sagsag.

Seawater is poured into the ash. The brine, called tasik, is collected and poured into clay pots. These are boiled for several hours in the furnace, continually replenishing the pots with more brine once some evaporate. Eventually, the pots will crack, revealing an orb-shaped solidified salt.

title: File:Cacao's Journey to the Philippines.jpg
desc: Considered "food for the gods" by civilizations in Mesoamerica, cacao arrived in the Philippines in the form of cocoa beans produced by Spanish Capuchin friars in Ecuador, through the Manila-Acapulco Galleon Trade that linked the Americas, Europe, and Asia from 1565 to 1815. Philippine cacao farmers cultivate three varieties: Criollo is the rarest and most expensive cacao native to Central and South America; Forastero is the most easily produced variety around the world; and Trinitario is the hybrid of the two.

title: File:Fishermen Philippines (17822795693).jpg
artist: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand
desc: Marine fishing in the Philippines in more than an industry; it is a way of life. With 7,100 islands, the Philippines has the world's longest discontinuous coastline. Over a million Filipinos are engaged in marine fishing. Of these, an estimated 800,000 are small-scale fishermen using tradition, low-cost techniques, notably net fishing from small boats and the fish corral. The fish corral is a stationary pen that traps fish in coastal fishing grounds. Traditionally, these techniques have provided small-scale fishermen and their families with a means of subsistence. In the past two decades, however, their way of life has been threatened by the rapid commercialization of Philippine waters.

title: File:R Fishermen. Philippines. (52598261812).jpg
artist: Bernard Spragg. NZ from Christchurch, New Zealand
desc:
A net makes a big difference. So can a team.

Though it may seem obvious, the contrast between line fishing and net fishing is dramatic. With line fishing you cast and wait, often alone, catching one at a time. But net fishing is a different activity altogether, offering the possibility of a much bigger catch. It even changes the fishermen’s expectations as they approach the water. Net fishermen form a team. They cast in groups and bring in a net full of fish together, relying upon one another for strength to draw it back in.

desc: OLONGAPO, Philippines (Dec. 8, 2024)—Volunteers with Military Sealift Command’s dry cargo and ammunition ship USNS Charles Drew (T-AKE 10), hand out food to children of the Niños Pag Asa Orphanage Center, during a community outreach event in Olongapo, Philippines, Dec. 8, 2024. MSC’s civilian mariners partnered with Olongapo local organizations and visited two centers for children to interact with kids and provide donations during a community outreach event.
